title: Data Cleaning and Validation
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and key terms of data cleaning and validation.
Apply identifying missing values in a small PostgreSQL-oriented example or design decision.
Validate the result against the expected behavior and identify one portability, safety, or edge-case consideration.

content.intro: Learn data cleaning and validation through a short explanation, a concept diagram, and a PostgreSQL-oriented example. Focus on the reason for the query or design decision before memorizing syntax.
content.why_it_matters: Data Cleaning and Validation matters because database behavior becomes more reliable when the intended row meaning, data shape, and edge cases are explicit. This lesson follows the SQL curriculum's listed subtopics and calls out PostgreSQL-specific behavior when it matters.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: A safe data cleaning and validation workflow separates ingestion from trusted production tables. Load into staging, validate encodings and data quality, reconcile counts, then apply well-defined changes in a transaction or restartable batch.

content_blocks.title: Apply the idea
content_blocks.text: Start with the subtopics: Identifying missing values, Detecting duplicate records, Standardizing text, Validating numeric and date ranges. Define the result you expect, run or inspect the small example in your own disposable PostgreSQL lab, and change one assumption at a time. The embedded lesson editor is a demonstration shell: the current project shows the sample expected output and does not execute arbitrary SQL on the server.

items.title: Identifying missing values
items.text: Identifying missing values requires deliberate handling of absent or unknown values. In SQL, NULL is not the same as zero or an empty string; use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL for direct tests and check how expressions and aggregates propagate unknowns.

items.title: Detecting duplicate records
items.text: Detecting duplicate records helps you move data through staging, bulk load/export, encoding checks, validation, cleansing, and incremental synchronization workflows. Start with a concrete example, state the expected result, and verify the behavior before extending the query or design.

items.title: Standardizing text
items.text: Standardizing text depends on text representation, collation, wildcard semantics, and sometimes locale. Test spaces, case, accents, Unicode, and special characters rather than assuming every database compares strings identically.

items.title: Validating numeric and date ranges
items.text: Validating numeric and date ranges needs a clearly defined time zone and calendar grain. Prefer typed date/time values over formatted strings, define inclusive/exclusive boundaries, and check daylight-saving or month-boundary cases where they matter.

items.title: Rejecting or quarantining invalid rows
items.text: Rejecting or quarantining invalid rows helps you move data through staging, bulk load/export, encoding checks, validation, cleansing, and incremental synchronization workflows. Start with a concrete example, state the expected result, and verify the behavior before extending the query or design.

content_blocks.code:
SELECT LOWER(TRIM(email)) AS normalized_email, COUNT(*) AS rows_seen
FROM customers
GROUP BY LOWER(TRIM(email))
ORDER BY rows_seen DESC, normalized_email;
content_blocks.expected_output: The query surfaces normalized email groups for quality review. A real ingestion pipeline should stage raw data and compare counts before applying a merge.

Do not use production credentials or a production database. Some specialist examples require optional extensions or a specific PostgreSQL version, as stated in the lesson. The CodeLeaf lesson Run button in this scaffold only previews the documented expected output; it is not a SQL execution service.
content_blocks.reset_steps: For queries, restore the original text and compare results. For statements that change data, use the transaction and rollback shown in the example, or recreate the disposable lab from the included setup instructions. Do not reset production data.

content_blocks.title: Remember
content_blocks.text: SQL correctness depends on data shape, constraints, NULL behavior, row counts, and the target database dialect—not just whether a statement parses.

hints: Begin with the subtopic identifying missing values and write down the result you expect.
Use the smallest valid example; verify table and column names before adding complexity.
Inspect one edge case: missing values, duplicate matches, tied sort values, a constraint violation, or an engine-specific syntax difference.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a query is correct because it returns some rows.
common_mistakes.why: A result can omit valid records, multiply joined rows, mishandle NULLs, or rely on a non-deterministic order.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected row grain, add targeted edge cases, and use a stable tie-breaker whenever order or pagination matters.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying PostgreSQL syntax into another SQL engine without checking support.
common_mistakes.why: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, and Oracle differ in types, functions, row limits, procedural features, and transaction behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Label the target engine/version and verify the relevant official reference before adapting the query.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing with production data or credentials.
common_mistakes.why: Practice statements can change rows or expose sensitive information if run against the wrong connection.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a dedicated disposable lab, check current_database() and current_user, and review all changes before committing.

summary: Data Cleaning and Validation is about making the database behavior and the expected result explicit.
Use the provided subtopics as a review checklist and validate a small test case.
Keep vendor-specific syntax, access assumptions, and production-safety boundaries visible.
